newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Madagascar's president says he will step down.
newsitem.headline: Madagascar's president says he will step down.

text.p: Madagascar's President Albert Zafy said on Thursday he would step down from the post after the constitutional court confirmed his impeachment and ordered the prime minister to take over until an election.
In an address to the nation, Zafy said he would step down on October 10 but he hit out at the head of the national assembly, Richard Andriamanjato, and the 99 deputies who voted for impeachment.

Zafy referred to the assassination in February 1975 of Colonel Richard Ratsimandrava after only six days as president and said that like him, he was the victim of a political clique opposed to his policies.
The High Constitutional Court, ruling on the parliamentary vote in July to impeach Zafy, on Thursday said it "declares the definitive impeachment of the president of the republic Albert Zafy".
The court said the order by parliament chief Andriamanjato for the impeachment of the head of state was regular and admissable on the grounds Zafy had violated the constitution.
The court noted the subsequent "vacancy in the post of president of the republic" and designated Prime Minister Norbert Ratsirahonana to take over his duties until a new head of state was elected.

Zafy accused Andriamanjato of backing a plan to dump toxic waste in Madagascar in return for up to $300 million and for supporting "parallel financing" opposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
He criticised parliamentarians for earning high salaries compared with the general poverty of the Malagasy people.
Before the court ruling, the next presidential election was scheduled for 1998, a year after parliamentary polls.
Zafy had said the constitutional court was not empowered to decide whether to dismiss him and had refused to accept the parliament vote in July by 99-32 in favour of his impeachment.
Only 92 votes, or two-thirds of all members of the national assembly, are needed for an impeachment motion to pass.
Parliament invoked what it said were Zafy's repeated violations of the constitution and accused him of acting against the interests of the people.
Zafy would not be barred from the new presidential election.
The crisis was a result of growing opposition to Zafy, who won Madagascar's multi-party elections in 1993, defeating former military ruler Didier Ratsiraka after 17 years in power.
But democracy brought no improvement in the material lives of the 14 million islanders, among the poorest people on earth.
Zafy, a 68-year-old professor of surgery and downbeat man of the people in his trademark straw hat, emerged as the figurehead of opposition to Ratsiraka in strikes and demonstrations in 1991.
Madagascar's army has pledged to uphold the constitution and rule of law during the crisis between parliament and Zafy.
The managing director of the IMF said during a visit earlier this year that he was shocked by Madagascar's economic decline since his last trip in 1991.
Before the visit Zafy had defended "parallel financing" -- private loans ostensibly for development projects but at higher interest rates than from multilateral donors such as the IMF.
Madagascar last month signed undertakings with the IMF and World Bank on reforms expected to pave the way for a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility and debt rescheduling.
Madagascar has a total foreign debt of some $4 billion.
Zafy won a referendum last September that gave him the power to name the prime minister instead of the national assembly.
